title: Jonah and the Silence
premise: After her mother's funeral, Wendell Ravensworth returns to the family house in coastal Maine to catalog a lifetime of silence — boxes of unlabeled photographs, letters never sent, and a father who left before she could form a memory of him. There she meets Maren Oduya, the last fluent speaker of Kivuli, a dying language, who asks Wendell to become her final student. As lessons deepen, Wendell discovers her mother secretly funded Maren's decades of exile and that her father's disappearance is entangled with a betrayal Maren has carried for fifty years. Learning Kivuli becomes an excavation of her own inheritance: identity, complicity, and the price of loyalty. In the end, Wendell must choose between protecting her family's reputation and speaking the truth aloud, recording Maren's testimony in a language only she will ever understand.
about_author: Lior Iversen is a former archivist who spent six years cataloging endangered-language recordings in university basements before turning to fiction. Their work explores what families refuse to say and what languages refuse to die quietly.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Three weeks after the funeral, she moves through her childhood home like a renter, cataloging rooms for an estate sale she keeps postponing. A neighbor mentions 'the woman on the point' her mother visited monthly for years. Emotional beat: numbness cracked by the first question she can't file away.

chapters.title: Boxes Without Labels
chapters.summary: Wendell finds photographs of her mother with a stranger at a shoreline cottage, dated across four decades, none labeled. Her father appears in exactly one image, face turned away. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: the archive of silence becomes physical, and she begins to resent her own inheritance.

chapters.title: The Woman on the Point
chapters.summary: Wendell walks the headland and finds Maren Oduya, elderly and sharp-eyed, tending a garden of plants from another continent. Maren recognizes her instantly: 'You have her hands.' She asks Wendell to be her last student. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: wary curiosity; the offer feels like a trap and a lifeline at once.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: The first lesson: greetings, names, the word for silence, which is also the word for snowfall. Maren teaches through objects, refusing English whenever possible. Wendell learns her mother's Kivuli name meant 'the one who listens.' POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: grief given a new grammar; tenderness toward a stranger.

chapters.title: What the Letters Didn't Say
chapters.summary: Interleaved POV: Maren, 1974, arriving in Maine as a young refugee linguist, meeting Wendell's mother Ruth at a library desk. A friendship forms over borrowed dictionaries. Emotional beat: warmth shadowed by something Maren refuses to name even in memory.

chapters.title: The Estate Lawyer
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The will contains an odd clause: a sealed envelope to be opened only 'when you can read it.' The lawyer knows nothing more. Wendell realizes her mother planned this convergence deliberately. Emotional beat: anger at being managed from beyond the grave, mixed with awe.

chapters.title: Vocabulary of Loss
chapters.summary: Lessons continue; Maren's health falters mid-session but she insists on finishing the verb conjugations. She reveals Kivuli has no future tense — only the near-now and the long-now. POV alternates Wendell and present-day Maren. Emotional beat: mortality entering the room, uninvited.

chapters.title: The Photograph Wendell Keeps
chapters.summary: Wendell studies the single image of her father and notices Maren's reflection in a window behind him. She confronts Maren, who goes silent for the first time — a silence Wendell now recognizes as deliberate, not empty. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: betrayal of trust; the student becomes interrogator.

chapters.title: Maren, 1976
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Wendell's father, Daniel, a young academic, offers to help Maren publish the first Kivuli grammar — then takes credit for it himself when his career stalls. Ruth discovers the theft. Emotional beat: the slow corrosion of admiration into powerlessness.

chapters.title: Ruth's Choice
chapters.summary: Maren's POV continues. Ruth confronts Daniel privately and chooses loyalty to her marriage over truth to her friend, paying Maren hush money disguised as a research grant. Maren accepts, and hates herself for it. Emotional beat: shame as a shared currency; both women corrupted by kindness misapplied.

chapters.title: The Long-Now
chapters.summary: Present day. Wendell, now conversant, reads old journal pages Maren kept in Kivuli and understands fragments: her mother's name appears beside the word for debt. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: the language becomes a key turning inside her; vertigo of inherited guilt.

chapters.title: A Visitor from the University
chapters.summary: A linguistics department representative arrives offering Maren a endowed chair if she signs away recording rights to a foundation — one tied, Wendell discovers, to her father's legacy trust. History threatening to repeat. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: protective fury; Wendell chooses Maren over the family name for the first time.

chapters.title: Conjugating Betrayal
chapters.summary: Maren finally tells Wendell the whole story aloud, in Kivuli, so that the confession exists in a language almost no one alive can parse. Wendell translates as she listens, becoming witness and accomplice simultaneously. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: catharsis and dread — a truth spoken is a truth that demands action.

chapters.title: The Sealed Envelope
chapters.summary: Wendell can now read enough. Inside the envelope: Ruth's full confession and a letter asking forgiveness not for the theft but for the silence. Wendell rages, grieves, and understands why her mother sent her to Maren. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: the stranger in the photographs becomes legible; forgiveness begins as comprehension.

chapters.title: Daniel Returns
chapters.summary: Wendell's father, elderly and diminished, arrives unannounced after learning of Ruth's death, seeking absolution or leverage — even he isn't sure which. He meets Maren in the garden. POV: Wendell observing. Emotional beat: terror and pity; power revealed as a costume worn too long.

chapters.title: The Grammar of Power
chapters.summary: Daniel offers Maren public restitution — a retraction, funding, her name restored — in exchange for her signing the foundation agreement. Maren asks Wendell, in Kivuli, what she thinks. Wendell answers in Kivuli: the truth is not a bargaining chip. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: the student speaks with authority for the first time.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Maren declines the offer and instead dictates her testimony to Wendell in full, to be deposited with the university under her own name regardless of consequence. Daniel leaves without absolution. POV: Maren. Emotional beat: liberation through exposure; fifty years of silence ending in a single afternoon.

chapters.title: Recording Session
chapters.summary: Wendell records Maren speaking Kivuli for eleven hours — stories, songs, curses, recipes, the word for snowfall. The archive becomes an act of love rather than ownership. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: devotion; the language passing from one pair of hands to another, however briefly.

chapters.title: The Last Fluent Speaker Sleeps
chapters.summary: Maren dies peacefully in early winter. Wendell, per her instructions, speaks the eulogy half in Kivuli, half in English, before a congregation that understands almost none of it and all of it. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: grief transfigured into responsibility.

chapters.title: Publication
chapters.summary: Wendell publishes the grammar under Maren's name alone, with Ruth's confession appended as historical record. Her father's institution retaliates; Wendell loses professional standing and does not care. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: cost accepted; truth chosen over belonging.

chapters.title: Snowfall / Silence
chapters.summary: One year later, Wendell lives in Maren's cottage, teaching a small Saturday class of curious neighbors — the language survives, changed, imperfect, alive. She forgives her mother fully and her father partially. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; inheritance rewritten.

chapters.title: The One Who Listens
chapters.summary: Final chapter. Wendell records herself speaking Kivuli — her own stories now, in the long-now tense — adding her voice to the archive for whoever comes next. The last line of the book is the Kivuli word for beginning, which is also the word for tide. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: continuity; silence transformed into speech.
